title: Population density, not corruption or ethnic conflict, is the ceiling on African development
dek: The author abandons mainstream explanations like corruption and ethnic conflict, arguing instead that Africa's independence-era population density of under 10 people per square kilometer is why urbanization, fiscal capacity, and infrastructure development never took off. East Asian policy models themselves, by contrast, are universally applicable.
why: An African development history that speaks through numbers and uses East Asian cases as constant reference points; central is Ethiopia, which internalized the East Asian model yet stumbled at crucial junctures—dense with insight throughout.
who: Founders, investors, and policy researchers tracking developmental economics, African markets, or questions about whether the China model can be replicated.

points.h: Africa's population density at independence was under ten people per square kilometer
points.body: The author notes that at World War II's end, Africa's area was vast enough to contain China, India, Europe, and the United States, yet had a population density below 10 people per square kilometer—compared to 50 in Southeast Asia and 70 in East Asia at the same time. Population density determines whether a market exists, whether cities can be sustained, and whether infrastructure costs can be spread across enough people to become economical. He illustrates with London's Elizabeth Line subway, newly built at a cost of $30 billion, affordable only because 1.5 million people live within a ten-minute walk of its stations. That density cannot be replicated elsewhere in Europe, let alone in Africa.

points.h: Elephants ate between one-quarter and one-third of Tanzania's crops each year
points.body: Disease and elephants were two concrete reasons African population density never grew. In the early 19th century, Africa was estimated to have 25 million elephants; because humans died of disease so quickly, elephant populations at one point reproduced faster than people. Colonial archives from Tanzania document that in the 1920s, elephants ate between one-quarter and one-third of crops yearly and proved impossible to control. Only in the 1970s were wild elephant populations finally managed.

points.h: Africa never underwent the land reforms that made East Asia urban
points.body: The first principle in How Asia Works is land reform, but Africa at independence was sparsely populated with little Cold War pressure on governments to outbid communists for peasant support—so the radical redistribution seen in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan never happened. Colonial white settlers' land mostly transferred directly to ruling elites' cronies rather than to farmers. South Africa's case is even more extreme: Black dispossession occurred 50-100 years before independence; even with forced seizure today, those with urban jobs cannot be expected to become subsistence farmers again.

points.h: Female literacy jumped from 5% to 48%—an underestimated achievement
points.body: Africa started independence with just 16% adult literacy, and only 5% among women—far below Taiwan and Korea's starting point of around 45%. The cause was the same: low-density colonial territories had no tax base, so colonizers refused to fund education, and sub-Saharan Africa had almost no public schools before the 1950s. Yet by 1995, female African literacy had reached 48%, surpassing the Indian subcontinent. The author argues this catch-up has been severely underestimated.

points.h: Meles treated development as an unquestionable national faith—like East Asia's
points.body: Former Ethiopian PM Meles carried books on agricultural development during his guerrilla war days, studying East Asian experience in the rainy season while fighting. His master's thesis, written at Erasmus, used Taiwan and South Korea as case studies. His policies were nearly textbook small-farmer-first: fertilizer, seeds, extension workers, rural roads, with the PM personally chairing agricultural meetings and awarding prizes to farmers. Grain output nearly tripled and extreme poverty fell from 69% to 31%. He believed in a kind of "development hegemony"—development as society's unthinking shared faith, the way he saw it in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and China.

points.h: Meles studied but failed to apply East Asia's competition and piloting principles
points.body: But Meles failed to learn two rules from the East Asian model: competition and piloting. He created METEC, a military-linked conglomerate, as a massive state enterprise monopolizing all ten sugar factory contracts without bidding; dam projects went straight to giant-scale implementation without the small-scale piloting that East Asia did first. What troubles the author most is that Meles' own thesis detailed Taiwan and Korea's private and competitive mechanisms, yet he never applied this to Ethiopia. By contrast, Zhu Rongji's approach with China's SOEs—not privatization but breaking them into competing entities—this "second-best but workable" logic Meles never replicated.

points.h: Xi Jinping urged Ethiopia's PM to abandon federalism for one-party rule
points.body: The 1995 federal constitution granted every ethnic state secession rights and printed ethnicity on identity cards—a system that essentially let the 6% Tigrayan elite hide in the shadows while controlling the military and security forces. During the 2013 G20, Xi Jinping told then-PM Hailemariam that he worried about Ethiopia and asked why it still had regional parties and why it didn't simply become one-party rule. Hailemariam had no answer. Seven years later, that ethnic federal system did explode into civil war killing roughly 600,000 people.

points.h: Chinese investment in Africa is profit-seeking, not grand strategy
points.body: The author stresses repeatedly that Chinese firms' and banks' behavior in Africa actually adapts to local conditions: they pay bribes when facing corrupt governments, and quote fairly when dealing with governments bent on delivery. But ultimately, what drives Chinese manufacturing to African investment is not grand strategy but domestic competition too intense and margins too low. Chinese industry finds African markets for basic products more profitable. Meanwhile, Sino-African trade's real problem is that China barely buys anything African—mainly just raw materials and commodities.
